1093.title: A mirror for meditation
1093.hook: the lists as a mirror: seeing which factors are present while sitting
1093.howItsDone: In insight meditation, some Theravada teachers have students note what arises in the mind with a soft label, such as restless or calm, and then return to the breath or the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a house in Myanmar, and the lists sung aloud over someone who had died. Your line: chanted and studied.

A father and his young son. The boy is Rahula, and the father is the Buddha. In one of the Majjhima suttas, the Buddha holds up the kind of question you'd ask a child: what is a mirror for? Rahula gives the plain answer. For looking at yourself. For seeing what's there. It's one image among several in that talk, and it hands this path a tool for the end of a long block of lists. All those factors, the restless ones, the bright ones, the dull ones: what are they for? One answer: they're a mirror.
screen: `A FATHER AND A SON.` → `WHAT IS A MIRROR FOR?` → `THE LISTS AS A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: First, the mirror in the sutta. After Rahula answers, the Buddha says, in paraphrase: in the same way, look at what you do. Before you act, while you act, and after, reflect on it. Is this leading to harm, for me or for anyone else? If it is, set it down. If it isn't, carry on, glad. A mirror is for checking, the way you'd check your face before you walk out the door. Second, the mirror while sitting. In the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, one thing a meditator watches is the mind itself. In paraphrase: a mind with greed is known as a mind with greed; a mind without it is known as a mind without it. The same with anger, with confusion, with a mind that's scattered or gathered. Nothing is added. You just see what's in the glass. Third, what the lists add. The suttas give the outline; the Abhidhamma fills in the detail: restlessness, doubt, sloth, envy; mindfulness, calm, softness, compassion. When you sit, those names can work like the edges of a mirror. Something stirs, and instead of a fog you can say: oh, that's restlessness. That's doubt. That's a small moment of calm. Fourth, what a mirror never does. It doesn't scold, and it doesn't flatter. It shows a smudge on your cheek the same way it shows your smile. Some teachers of this practice stress that the naming is for seeing, not for grading. A factor in the glass isn't a verdict on you. It's what's there this moment, and the next moment may show something else.
screen: `BEFORE, WHILE, AND AFTER YOU ACT.` · `A MIND WITH GREED, KNOWN AS SUCH.` · `THE LISTS GIVE THE GLASS EDGES.` · then, large: `A MIRROR DOESN'T SCOLD.`

segments.voice: Let the breath go at its own pace, and when something shows up in the mind, give it one quiet name, the way you'd read a label: restless, tired, curious, doubt, calm. Don't chase it away or hold on to it. If no name fits, just say, something, and come back to the breath.
A mirror for meditation. The lists of mental factors used the way the Buddha told Rahula to use a mirror: to see what's there, without scolding. Today's word.
Your line: a mirror. It shows the smudge and the smile the same way, and it never scolds. Same time tomorrow.

1094.title: A day of factors
1094.hook: noticing mental factors through a whole ordinary day
1094.howItsDone: Some meditation teachers ask students to bring mindfulness into daily tasks such as walking, eating and washing, and some monasteries ring a bell during the day as a reminder to return to the present moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahula and the mirror, held up while you sit to see what's there. Your line: a mirror.

The alarm goes off. A flash of something: dread, or relief that it's Saturday. The kettle. A headline on the phone, and the jaw tightens. A message from a friend, and it loosens. The car won't start, or the toddler won't wear the blue socks. A long meeting where the mind wanders out the window. A kind word from a stranger at the store. Dishes. Bed. Nobody would call that day a meditation. But every one of those moments had factors in it, the same ones the Abhidhamma lists. Today the mirror comes off the cushion.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE KETTLE, THE HEADLINE.` → `A KIND WORD, THE DISHES.` → `THE MIRROR, OFF THE CUSHION.`

segments.voice: First, the suttas already point here. In the great teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, attention doesn't stop when the sitting stops. In paraphrase: going out and coming back, looking ahead and looking around, bending and stretching, putting on the robe, eating, drinking, chewing, even in the bathroom, the practitioner acts with clear knowing. Getting dressed counts. Lunch counts. Second, the Abhidhamma gives that clear knowing something to look for. Remember the seven factors it says are in every moment of mind: contact, feeling, perception, intention, one-pointedness, life, attention. So there's never a moment with nothing to notice. The kettle has contact and feeling in it. So does the headline. Third, the colors change through the day. Some moments carry restlessness or envy or dullness. Others carry calm, gladness, a flicker of compassion. Watched across a whole day, the mind looks less like one fixed mood and more like weather: a squall at nine, sun at noon, fog in the afternoon meeting. That's what the lists have been saying all along: mind is many, and each state passes. Fourth, a simple tool. Once an hour, stop for one breath and ask: what three factors are here right now? Maybe tired, curious, a little irritated. Maybe hungry, focused, glad. You don't need the Pali names, and you don't need to get it right. By evening you'd have a small map of one day, drawn from the inside.

segments.voice: Take a few easy breaths and ask: what three factors are here right now? Wait for them instead of hunting: maybe a feeling, pleasant or unpleasant or neither, maybe a mood like boredom or ease, maybe attention itself, landing on the breath. Name all three quietly, then let them go and sit with the breath.
A day of factors. Carrying the Abhidhamma's mirror through an ordinary day, and noticing which factors come and go, from the alarm to bedtime. Today's word.
Your line: a day of noticing. From the alarm to the dishes, no moment is empty of something to see. See you tomorrow.

1095.title: What it is not
1095.hook: the Abhidhamma is one way of looking, not a test anyone must pass
1095.howItsDone: In Theravada communities, some monks and lay people devote years to studying the Abhidhamma, while others give their practice mainly to meditation; the tradition honors both study and insight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mirror carried through a whole ordinary day, three factors once an hour. Your line: a day of noticing.

Fifty-two mental factors. Twenty-eight kinds of matter. Twenty-four conditions. After all these lists, a fair question rises up: does a person have to learn all this? Is there an exam at the end of the path, a long sheet of Pali with blanks to fill in? The Theravada tradition has its own answer, and it comes in a story about an old man who never opened the books.
screen: `FIFTY-TWO, TWENTY-EIGHT, TWENTY-FOUR.` → `IS THERE AN EXAM?` → `AN OLD MAN WITHOUT THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, two duties. In the commentary on the Dhammapada, a man who has become a monk late in life asks the Buddha what the duties are in this teaching. There are two, the story says. One is the duty of the books: learning the texts, studying, keeping the words. The other is the duty of insight: watching body and mind until you see how they really are. Second, the old monk chooses. In paraphrase: I came to this late, I'm too old for the books, teach me the second. He's taught a meditation practice and goes off to sit, and the story goes on to tell how far he went with it. Nobody in the story tells him he chose wrong. Both duties are honored, and the Theravada tradition has kept both: monks and lay people who study the lists closely, and monks and lay people whose whole practice is the sitting. Third, the lists aren't one fixed answer. The Sarvastivada, the other school, counts some things differently. Two careful traditions, looking at the same mind, drew two maps. A map is a way of looking. It isn't the ground you walk on. Fourth, what that leaves. The Abhidhamma is a gift some people love: precise, patient, endless. For others it's a mirror they pick up now and then. For some it never comes off the shelf. None of that is a pass or a fail. The test, if there is one, is the old monk's: does the looking help you see?
screen: `TWO DUTIES: BOOKS AND INSIGHT.` · `THE OLD MONK CHOOSES THE SITTING.` · `TWO SCHOOLS DREW TWO MAPS.` · then, large: `A WAY OF LOOKING, NOT A TEST.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand open on your knee, palm up and loose, as if a small list were lying in it that you could close your fingers around or let slide off. Sit with the breath, and if a name comes, restless, calm, doubt, let it sit on the open palm without gripping it or throwing it away.
What it is not. The Abhidhamma isn't an exam the path sets. It's one way of looking, honored alongside the duty of simply sitting and seeing. Today's word.
Your line: one way of looking. The books and the sitting are both honored, and neither is a test. Rest well.

1096.title: Abhidhamma, closed
1096.hook: mind, factors, matter, conditions, in plain words
1096.howItsDone: Students of the Abhidhamma in Theravada countries may learn it from a short manual such as the Abhidhammattha Sangaha before turning to the seven books themselves, and some teachers use its lists alongside meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an old monk who chose the sitting over the books, and nobody told him he was wrong. Your line: one way of looking.

Back to the watchmaker's bench where this block began. Springs, gears, a tiny wheel, a jewel no bigger than a grain of sand, laid out on a cloth. Taken apart, it looks nothing like the thing on your wrist. And yet that's the only way to see how it keeps time. This block of the path did the same with a person: it laid a single moment open on the cloth and named the parts. Today the cloth gets folded up, before the path turns somewhere new.
screen: `BACK TO THE WATCHMAKER'S BENCH.` → `A MOMENT, LAID OPEN.` → `THE CLOTH FOLDED UP.`

segments.voice: First, where it sits. The Abhidhamma is the third basket of the Pali canon, the one you met on day two hundred ninety-two: seven books, from the list of mental states to the great book of conditions. Theravada tradition says the Buddha first taught it to his mother in a heaven, and in Myanmar it's still chanted for the dead and studied by lay people. Second, mind. Two ways of speaking: the everyday way, with people and tables, and the ultimate way, with moments. In the ultimate way, the mind is a stream of tiny moments, each arising and passing. A mango falls on a sleeping man, and seeing it, smelling it, eating it, is a whole chain of moments in a flash. Third, factors. Each moment is colored. Seven factors, the texts say, are in every moment: contact, feeling, perception and the rest. Then the troubled ones: restlessness, greed, conceit, envy, dullness, doubt. And the beautiful ones: mindfulness, conscience, calm, softness, compassion, gladness. Fourth, matter and conditions. Matter begins with the four great elements, earth, water, fire and air, and the body's own warmth and life. And nothing stands alone: the great book of relations traces how each thing holds up the next, through roots, supports, friends, food, weather. Then the view widened: debates, another school's lists, a mirror, a day of noticing, one way of looking. All of it from one idea: look closely enough, and what seemed solid turns out to be made of the smallest parts, each arising, each passing, each leaning on the others.
screen: `THE THIRD BASKET, SEVEN BOOKS.` · `MIND: A STREAM OF MOMENTS.` · `FACTORS: TROUBLED AND BEAUTIFUL.` · then, large: `MATTER, AND EVERYTHING RELATES.`

segments.voice: Let the lists from this block drift past slowly, like cards turned over on a table: the seven in every moment, the troubled ones, the beautiful ones, the four great elements, the roots and supports. Don't sort them; just notice which one your mind keeps coming back to, because that's the one to keep. Say its name once, quietly, and rest with the breath.
Abhidhamma. The higher teaching: mind, factors, matter and conditions, the teaching broken down into its smallest parts. Today's word, and the close of this block.
Your line: the smallest parts. Tomorrow the path turns to the great vehicle. I'll be here tomorrow.

1097.title: The great vehicle
1097.hook: the name the Mahayana gave itself; Buddhists today avoid the old contrast term and say Theravada instead
1097.howItsDone: Mahayana is the name used for the Buddhist traditions of China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Tibet, among others; Buddhists today refer to the tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia as Theravada.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the higher teaching folded up: mind, factors, matter, conditions. Your line: the smallest parts. Today a new block begins.

A big old house is on fire, and the father is outside. His children are still in there, playing, too absorbed to notice the smoke. He shouts, and they don't come. So he tries something else. He calls out that carts are waiting at the gate, the kind they've always wanted: one pulled by goats, one by deer, one by an ox. The children come running out. And when they're safe, he doesn't give them those three. He gives each child one great cart, finer than any of them asked for. That story comes from the Lotus Sutra, and its word for those carts is in today's name.
screen: `A HOUSE ON FIRE.` → `THREE CARTS AT THE GATE.` → `ONE GREAT CART FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: You met these sutras arriving on day eight hundred seventy-five. Today, their name. First, the vehicle. The Sanskrit word is yana: a cart, a vehicle, the thing that carries you somewhere. Buddhist teachers used it for a path, the way across. In the parable, the three carts stand for different paths of practice, and the one great cart for the single vehicle the sutra says they all lead into. Second, the name. Communities who treasured sutras like the Lotus called their way Mahayana. Maha means great: the great vehicle, wide enough to carry all beings. That's the name they gave themselves, and it's the name used here. Third, the hard part. Some Mahayana texts also used a contrast term for other paths: a lesser, or small, vehicle. It was a word for someone else, not a name anyone took for themselves. The Buddhists of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia call their own tradition Theravada, the way of the elders. Buddhists today avoid the old contrast term and say Theravada instead, and so will this path; when the old term shows up in a text, it's there as history. Fourth, what that habit teaches. A name someone gives you can carry a judgment inside it. A name you give yourself carries what you love. Mahayana, Theravada, and the schools ahead on this path, Zen, Pure Land, the Tibetan traditions, will each be called here by the name they use. No ranking, just each by its own name.

1098.title: How it began
1098.hook: new sutras appear in the early centuries CE; scholars still debate where and how
1098.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists receive the great-vehicle sutras as the Buddha's word and recite, copy and study them, while historians continue to debate where and how the texts first appeared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a burning house, three carts promised, and one great cart given. Your line: each by its own name.

Where did it come from? Ask a historian about the Mahayana, and the honest answer starts with a shrug. New sutras appear in the early centuries of the common era. But who first recited them, in what kind of place, among what kind of people? The record doesn't settle it. Scholars have argued about it for a long time and still do. That might sound like a gap. Today it's the lesson: a beginning that is still debated, and how to hold a question that won't close.
screen: `WHERE DID IT COME FROM?` → `THE RECORD DOESN'T SETTLE IT.` → `A QUESTION THAT WON'T CLOSE.`

segments.voice: First, what the sutras themselves say. They open the old way: thus have I heard. The Buddha is teaching, a crowd is listening. Those who keep these texts receive them as the Buddha's word, and that is how they're read in Mahayana communities today. Second, the places scholars have looked. Some look to the forest: monks living apart, meditating hard, perhaps seeing visions, and bringing back teachings. Some look to the stupas, the shrines where lay people came with flowers and lamps, and ask whether devotion there shaped the new movement. Others point to ordinary monasteries of the older schools, where monks drawn to the new sutras may have kept the same rules and lived under the same roof as everyone else. When Chinese pilgrims later traveled through India, their accounts mention followers of the great vehicle and of other schools in the same regions, sometimes in the same places. Third, a clue inside the books. Some of the new sutras talk about themselves. The Lotus Sutra praises those who keep it, read it, recite it and copy it out. A text that asks to be copied expects to travel. Some scholars think the books themselves were part of the answer, carried and honored like a shrine. Fourth, what a careful person does with all this: holds it open. Several of these ideas may be partly true at once. Nobody has to choose a winner today, and Buddhists don't need the historians' answer to read a sutra. The beginning is still debated. That's an honest place to stand.

segments.voice: This week: the mirror, a day of noticing, one way of looking, the higher teaching folded up, the great vehicle, and yesterday, a beginning that's still debated. Your line: still debated.

A splinter in your foot. Nobody has to call a meeting about it. Your hand doesn't stop to ask whether the foot deserves help, or whether this is really the hand's problem. It just reaches down and pulls the thing out. A Buddhist poet named Shantideva leaned on that same plain fact, the hand looking after the foot, to explain the figure at the heart of the great vehicle: the one who sets out to wake up, not for themselves alone, but for everyone.

segments.voice: First, the word. Bodhisattva. Bodhi is awakening. Sattva is usually explained as a being. An awakening being, or a being set on awakening. This path met the word long ago in the Jataka tales, where it names the Buddha in his earlier lives, and Theravada Buddhists honor that path too. In the great vehicle, it becomes a path many are invited to walk. Second, where it starts. Mahayana teachers speak of bodhicitta, the mind of awakening, which you met on day three hundred twelve: the moment a person's wish for freedom turns outward and includes everyone. Shantideva's long poem, The Way of the Bodhisattva, is largely about that turn: how to give rise to that mind, guard it, and keep it from going out. Third, the body. In the poem Shantideva asks, in paraphrase: why protect one person's pain and not another's? The hand protects the foot because they're one body. Many limbs, one body. So too, he says, with beings. Their suffering isn't someone else's business any more than your foot is someone else's foot. He even practices trading places in his imagination, putting himself where another person stands, and looking back. Fourth, how it's lived. In Mahayana communities, people recite vows to free all beings, and the vow is not meant to be finished by Friday. It's a direction more than a task. For the sake of all can look like large things. It can also look like a hand reaching down for a foot, quickly, without a meeting.

segments.voice: Feel your hands resting and your feet on the floor, and notice how they belong to one body. Then let the circle grow, to the people in your home, on your street, people you'll never meet, and ask quietly what one small thing could help, even a little, beyond yourself. Wait for an answer that's simple and real, and hold it.
